extracted.intended_audience: legislators, political reformers, students of political theory and electoral reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and procedural rules for designing parliamentary elections: mode of voting (secret vs public), ballot administration, candidate expenses, accessibility of polling, member remuneration, and length of parliamentary terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect election vs direct election
rubrics_metrics.description: Every benefit of indirect election which is attainable at all is attainable under direct; indirect election is an additional and superfluous wheel in the machinery, has decided inferiority as a means of cultivating public spirit and political intelligence, prevents voter identifying with his representative, and places election in the hands of a comparatively small number of persons, affording great facilities to intrigue and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid schemes of indirect election for ordinary parliamentary representation because they reduce accountability and increase opportunities for bribery and intrigue; the evil is proportional to the discretion left to the chosen electors. Exceptionally, indirect election may be defensible in circumstances similar to the election of United States senators (i.e., special institutional contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of voting — secrecy vs publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of greatest moment is that of secrecy or publicity: 'Secrecy is justifiable in many cases, imperative in some ... but these cases, in affairs of a political character, are the exception, not the rule.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer publicity for political elections because secrecy fosters the impression that the suffrage is for the voter's private benefit rather than a public trust; reserve secret voting for exceptional circumstances (e.g., where coercion is extreme or voters are effectively enslaved).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional spirit and the civic meaning of voting
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit of an institution — the impression it makes on the mind of the citizen — is one of the most important parts of its operation. The spirit of vote by ballot is likely to be interpreted as the suffrage being 'for his particular use and benefit, and not as a trust for the public.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design voting rules with attention to the conveyed moral meaning: practices that suggest voting is a private right encourage self-interested behavior, whereas practices that emphasize public accountability encourage conscientious public-minded voting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting should be performed under public scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of voting, like any other public duty, should be performed under the eye and criticism of the public; every member of the public has an interest in its performance and a title to consider himself wronged if it is performed otherwise than honestly and carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use publicity to harness social sanction, compel deliberation, and make voters 'have to defend themselves to others'; departures from this principle must be strikingly exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: When secret ballot is defensible — protection against coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest case for the ballot is when the mischievous power of the Few over the Many is increasing; in oligarchic or highly coercive conditions the ballot can erect barriers against abuse of the franchise (historical examples: decline of Roman republic, certain Athenian uses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply secret ballot as a protective measure in contexts of clear, systemic coercion or intimidation; in more advanced states where coercive power is declining, the protective value of secrecy diminishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret voting increases opportunity for selfish or shame-free misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: As coercion declines, the greater source of evil is the selfishness or selfish partialities of the voter himself; the ballot would enable him to yield to such influences 'free from all sense of shame or responsibility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the declining risk from external coercion against growing risks of private selfish voting; when the latter predominates, publicity is the lesser evil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of filling voting papers at home or by post
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal allowing voting papers to be filled up at the voter's own residence, and sent by post, or called for by a public officer, is regarded as fatal because the act would be done in the absence of salutary and the presence of pernicious influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disallow remote completion and submission of ballots (postal/home voting) because they remove the protective influence of public presence and open opportunities for bribery and intimidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature on voting paper at public polling-place
rubrics_metrics.description: It is indispensable that the signature of the elector should be affixed to the paper at a public polling-place, or if there be no such place conveniently accessible, at some office open to all the world, and in the presence of a responsible public officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require elector identification/signature at a public place or open office to ensure accountability and to prevent private coercion and bribery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility of polling places and public provision of polling machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Polling places should be so numerous as to be within easy reach of every voter; no expenses of conveyance, at the cost of the candidate, should be tolerated. Hustings, poll clerks, and all the necessary machinery of elections should be at the public charge. The infirm, and they only on medical certificate, should have the right of claiming suitable carriage conveyance at the cost of the state or of the locality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure polling stations are widely accessible and that essential election administration costs are borne publicly to minimize candidate influence and barriers to voting; limit public‑funded conveyance to medically certified infirm voters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit candidate campaign expenses and require deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: The candidate should not be permitted to incur any but a limited and trifling expense for his election. Mr. Hare thinks it desirable that a sum of L50 should be required from every one who places his name on the list of candidates ... For all necessary expenses of this kind the L50 proposed ... ought to be sufficient. Any expenses beyond the deposit ... should be illegal and punishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a modest deposit (e.g., L50 or L100) to deter frivolous candidacies and restrict allowable campaign spending to the deposit; make excess expenditures illegal and subject to penalty to curb expensive elections that privilege the wealthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath/declaration and penalties to enforce expenditure limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration on oath or honor should be required from every member, on taking his seat, that he had not expended, nor would expend, money or money's worth beyond the L50 (or L100); if the assertion were proved false or the pledge broken, he should be liable to the penalties of perjury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require sworn statements about election expenditures and attach serious penalties (perjury) to falsehoods to change public norms and deter corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition/limitation of candidate-financed voter conveyance and canvassing expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: No expenses of conveyance, at the cost of the candidate, should be tolerated under any pretext. If the friends of the candidate choose to go to expense for committees and canvassing, there are no means of preventing them; but such expenses out of the candidate's own pocket, or any expenses whatever beyond the deposit of L50 (or L100), should be illegal and punishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbid candidate-funded transport for voters and limit candidate-funded campaign activities to what can be covered by the official deposit; accept that supporters may incur independent expenses but penalize circumvention by candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment of members — indemnity, not salary
rubrics_metrics.description: The payment of members of Parliament should be an indemnity for loss of time or money, not a salary. No remuneration which would make the occupation attractive as a paid profession should be attached, for that would attract adventurers and demoralize the office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If support is needed for capable persons without means, use limited indemnities or public subscription for exceptional cases rather than a regular salary that turns parliamentary office into a paid profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance tenure length to ensure responsibility and development of reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Members ought not to have so long a tenure as to make them forget their responsibility ... On the other hand, he should have such a term of office to look forward to as will enable him to be judged, not by a single act, but by his course of action. It is impossible to fix, by any universal rule, the boundary between these principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set parliamentary terms to strike a balance between frequent accountability (preventing neglect and loss of touch) and providing enough time for representatives to demonstrate sustained qualities and independence; adjust term length according to the strength of democratic power and susceptibility of representatives to nonpopular influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combatting electoral corruption requires serious legislative will
rubrics_metrics.description: There has never yet been, among political men, any real and serious attempt to prevent bribery, because there has been no real desire that elections should not be costly ... Opinion tolerates a false disclaimer only when it already tolerates the thing disclaimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislate and enforce penalties seriously (and publicly) to change norms; mere nominal prohibitions are ineffective without demonstrable legislative commitment and willingness to punish corruption.
